title: How your bean becomes a proxy
summary: A BeanPostProcessor swaps your object for a subclass or an interface implementation on the way out of the container. Four classes decide everything about how the feature behaves afterwards.
entry: Put a breakpoint in AbstractAutoProxyCreator.wrapIfNecessary and start an app with any @Transactional bean. It fires once per bean at startup.

steps.notice: The whole of Spring AOP hangs off one BeanPostProcessor callback. It returns a different object than it was given, and the container stores that instead. Nothing else in Spring needs to know.
Decides whether this bean needs proxying at all, by asking which advisors match it. A bean with no matching advisor is returned untouched, which is why most beans are not proxies.
JDK or CGLIB, in about ten lines. proxyTargetClass, whether the user supplied interfaces, and whether the target is itself an interface. Boot forces the CGLIB branch by default.

Builds the subclass. Note it goes through Objenesis, so no constructor runs and the proxy's own fields stay unset. That is the reason reading a field off an injected bean can give null while the getter works.

Every advised call enters here, and only calls that arrive through the proxy reference do. A call from one method of the target to another never reaches this frame, which is self-invocation in one sentence.
Walks the advisor chain, re-entering itself once per advice. Set a breakpoint here on a bean that is transactional and cached and you can watch the ordering that @Order on the advisors decided.

The escape hatch. With exposeProxy = true the proxy is put in a ThreadLocal so the target can call back through itself. It throws rather than returning null when exposeProxy is off, which is the right kind of failure.
